blocks.text: iOS 4 established several interaction patterns that would persist across later releases: eligible devices gained third-party multitasking services and fast app switching, users could group apps into folders, and Mail added a unified inbox, quick account switching, threaded conversations, and compatible-app attachment handling.

The release also brought iBooks to iPhone and iPod touch, introduced iAd, and expanded enterprise deployment, management, data protection, passcode, Exchange, and VPN capabilities. Apple’s security bulletin separately records repairs across privacy boundaries, device locking, media parsers, Safari, and WebKit.

Apple announced in early July that its signal-strength display formula could show too many bars. It planned a free software update using a revised calculation and larger lower bars, without changing the underlying radio signal.

blocks.text: Apple’s later iOS 4.0.2 advisory names iOS 4.0.1 as an affected predecessor, confirming that the version existed. Neither reviewed page names iOS 4.0.1 as the delivery vehicle for the earlier plan, and Apple’s 2010 security index does not list a 4.0.1 security release, so the linkage remains explicitly partial.
Apple’s dedicated advisory identifies two corrections in iOS 4.0.2. One added bounds checking to FreeType’s handling of embedded CFF font instructions, where a malicious PDF could execute code.

The second correction tightened IOSurface property validation to prevent code already running as the user from exploiting an integer overflow to gain system privileges. Apple’s 2010 index dates the release to August 11, 2010.

The public release brought Game Center’s friend challenges, automatic matchmaking, achievements, leaderboards, and game discovery to supported devices. On the new iPod touch, iOS 4.1 also underpinned FaceTime video calling alongside multitasking and folders.

citations.locator: Game Center, FaceTime, and September 8 update

blocks.text: Apple’s security bulletin documents a VoiceOver correction for location-service indicators, stronger certificate handling for FaceTime calls, safer TIFF and GIF parsing, and numerous WebKit memory-safety fixes. These entries are representative rather than a one-record-per-CVE transcription.

Apple’s announcement describes the November 22 package as iOS 4.2, while the local catalog and Apple’s later 4.3 advisory identify the installed predecessor as 4.2.1. The update brought multitasking, folders, unified Mail, and Game Center to iPad and introduced AirPlay and AirPrint across supported devices.

The release also made Find My iPhone, iPad, or iPod touch free on qualifying devices and expanded Safari search, enterprise management, accessibility, and language coverage on iPad. Apple’s bulletin records protections for configuration profiles, fonts and images, ad-triggered calls, networking, passcode state, credentials, and WebKit.

blocks.text: The feature release accelerated Safari JavaScript with Nitro, streamed a local Mac or PC iTunes library through Home Sharing, expanded AirPlay to more app, website, Photos, and iTunes content, and added Personal Hotspot for eligible iPhone 4 plans. It also let iPad owners assign the side switch to rotation lock or mute.

Apple’s security advisory records fixes for crafted fonts and images, XML parsing, IPv6 address privacy, Safari cookie and URL-handler behavior, WebKit memory safety, and Wi-Fi frame validation. The local March 9 date agrees with Apple’s security index but precedes the March 11 date originally announced by Newsroom.

blocks.text: Contemporaneous reporting preserved four items from the iOS 4.3.1 update notice: a sporadic graphics problem on the fourth-generation iPod touch, activation and connectivity trouble on certain cellular networks, image flicker with the Apple Digital AV Adapter on some televisions, and authentication failures involving some enterprise web services.

blocks.text: The same report dates the public release to March 25, 2011. Apple’s surviving first-party security corpus independently establishes iOS 4.3.1 as the predecessor covered by the iOS 4.3.2 advisory, but Apple’s archived security index does not preserve a separate 4.3.1 entry. The structured notes therefore rely on the cited contemporary report rather than presenting that material as a surviving Apple web page.

blocks.text: The trust-policy change rejected a set of fraudulently issued SSL certificates that could otherwise support interception of credentials or other sensitive information by an attacker in a privileged network position.

The update also stopped an XPath function from exposing heap addresses, corrected a QuickLook memory-corruption issue in Microsoft Office file handling, and fixed two WebKit flaws involving node sets and text-node lifetime. Apple’s index dates the package to April 14, 2011.

On April 27 Apple said an upcoming iOS update would reduce the cached Wi-Fi-hotspot and cell-tower database, stop backing it up, and delete it when Location Services was disabled. Apple characterized the oversized cache and continued updates after disabling Location Services as bugs.

The later iOS 4.3.4 advisory explicitly lists systems through iOS 4.3.3, confirming the version existed before July. Neither source names the promised privacy update as 4.3.3 or verifies the local May 4 date, so this batch records the two-source boundary only as partially documented context rather than as an unqualified delivery claim.

Two CoreGraphics corrections addressed FreeType handling of TrueType and Type 1 fonts inside malicious PDF files. Apple documented application termination or arbitrary code execution as possible outcomes.

The update also corrected an invalid type conversion in IOMobileFrameBuffer queueing primitives that could allow code already running as the user to gain system privileges. Apple’s index dates the release to July 15, 2011.

Apple corrected certificate-chain validation for X.509 certificates. The prior behavior could let an attacker in a privileged network position capture or alter data in SSL/TLS sessions and could permit other certificate-validation attacks.
The package improved validation of X.509 certificate chains and appears in Apple’s archived security index on July 25, 2011.

events.summary: The public iOS 4 release introduced multitasking services, folders, a reorganized Mail experience, iBooks, expanded enterprise controls, iAd, and a broad security repair set.

changes.title: Third-party multitasking services
changes.canonicalSummary: Eligible devices gained fast app switching and system services for selected background work.
changes.summary: Apple exposed seven multitasking services, including background audio and VoIP handling, while describing battery life and foreground performance as design constraints; hardware eligibility varied.

changes.title: Folders and home-screen customization
changes.canonicalSummary: Users could organize apps into named folders and choose wallpaper for the home and lock screens.
changes.summary: Dragging one app onto another created an automatically named, editable folder, while wallpaper selection expanded from the lock screen to the home screen.

changes.title: Unified and threaded Mail
changes.canonicalSummary: Mail added a unified inbox, fast inbox switching, conversation threads, and compatible-app attachment opening.
changes.summary: Multiple accounts could be viewed together or switched quickly, related messages could be grouped by conversation, and attachments could open in supporting App Store apps.

changes.title: iBooks on iPhone and iPod touch
changes.canonicalSummary: Apple extended its ebook reader and store to iPhone and iPod touch with synchronized reading state and PDF support.
changes.summary: The free iBooks app synchronized reading position, bookmarks, highlights, and notes for the same book and could store and display PDFs.

changes.title: Expanded enterprise management and protection
changes.canonicalSummary: iOS 4 added mobile-device management integration, wireless in-house app distribution, stronger data protection, and broader enterprise compatibility.
changes.summary: Administrators gained remote configuration, query, lock, and wipe integration; enterprises could distribute internal apps wirelessly; and the release added passcode-based protection, complex passcodes, multiple Exchange accounts, Exchange 2010, and forthcoming SSL VPN support.

changes.title: iAd application advertising platform
changes.canonicalSummary: iOS 4 introduced an in-app advertising platform designed to present interactive media without moving users into Safari.
changes.summary: Developers could embed iAd placements whose interactive or video presentation remained inside the host app, with Apple responsible for serving the advertisements.

changes.title: Photo-library location privacy boundary
changes.canonicalSummary: The application sandbox stopped apps from directly reading the photo library to infer visited locations without authorization.
changes.summary: Apple changed sandbox access so an application could not bypass location permission by directly examining geotagged photo-library data.

changes.title: Find My iPhone disabled-service enforcement
changes.canonicalSummary: Disabling Find My iPhone also disabled remote wipe and remote message display for that service.
changes.summary: The prior state could leave destructive remote actions available to someone with the MobileMe password even when device location was disabled; the update aligned those controls.

changes.title: Passcode lock-state protections
changes.canonicalSummary: The release tightened remote-lock passcode handling and computer-pairing checks around locked or recently booted devices.
changes.summary: Apple corrected a remote-lock state that could leave a passcode pre-entered and a short boot-time race that could permit computer pairing after an earlier unlocked shutdown.

changes.title: Image parser memory safety
changes.canonicalSummary: ImageIO received validation and memory-safety repairs for BMP, TIFF, JPEG, and other crafted image input.
changes.summary: The bulletin documents both possible memory disclosure and potential code execution when processing malicious image files; the release added initialization, validation, memory handling, and bounds checks.

changes.title: Safari cookie and URL trust cues
changes.canonicalSummary: Safari applied cookie preferences immediately and improved warnings or displayed URLs around potentially deceptive navigation.
changes.summary: The changes enforced updated cookie settings without waiting for restart, warned before visiting URLs containing embedded credentials, and corrected the address shown with certificate warnings after redirects.

changes.title: WebKit origin and memory-safety repairs
changes.canonicalSummary: WebKit fixed cross-origin data boundaries, cross-site scripting paths, information disclosure, and multiple memory-corruption conditions.
changes.summary: Apple’s bulletin describes a large browser repair set spanning cross-origin requests, malformed and encoded content, redirects, DOM and layout operations, and crafted pages that could terminate the browser or execute code.

events.summary: The surviving Apple record establishes iOS 4.0.1 as the predecessor to iOS 4.0.2 and separately describes a planned signal-bar formula correction, but it does not explicitly connect that correction to the 4.0.1 package.

changes.title: Signal-bar display correction with incomplete version linkage
changes.canonicalSummary: Apple documented a planned correction to the formula and sizing used for signal bars, while the surviving first-party pages do not explicitly name iOS 4.0.1 as its delivery vehicle.
changes.summary: The intended change was to make displayed bars better reflect existing signal strength and enlarge the lower three bars. Attaching it to this route is marked partially documented because Apple’s statement predates the package and omits its version number.

changes.title: Crafted PDF font bounds checking
changes.canonicalSummary: FreeType added bounds checks for CFF font instructions embedded in PDF documents.
changes.summary: The flaw could allow arbitrary code execution when viewing a malicious PDF containing a crafted embedded font.

changes.title: IOSurface privilege boundary
changes.canonicalSummary: IOSurface property handling gained bounds checks for an integer overflow that could enable system privileges.
changes.summary: Apple described the prerequisite as malicious code already running with user privileges; the corrected validation prevented that code from escalating through IOSurface.

events.summary: iOS 4.1 introduced Game Center to the public release line, expanded FaceTime support on the new iPod touch, and delivered security fixes for accessibility, FaceTime trust, image parsing, and WebKit.

blocks.text: The public release brought Game Center’s friend challenges, automatic matchmaking, achievements, leaderboards, and game discovery to supported devices. On the new iPod touch, iOS 4.1 also underpinned FaceTime video calling alongside multitasking and folders.

changes.title: Game Center social gaming network
changes.canonicalSummary: Game Center added friend challenges, matchmaking, achievements, leaderboards, and game discovery.
changes.summary: Supported games could connect players with friends or automatically selected opponents while surfacing scores, achievements, and games played by friends.

changes.title: FaceTime support on the new iPod touch
changes.canonicalSummary: iOS 4.1 enabled FaceTime video calls on the camera-equipped fourth-generation iPod touch.
changes.summary: The new iPod touch could place Wi-Fi FaceTime calls to another compatible iPod touch or iPhone 4 and switch between front and rear cameras.

changes.title: VoiceOver announcement for location use
changes.canonicalSummary: VoiceOver began announcing the settings indicator for apps that had recently requested location.
changes.summary: The change made the location-services status cue available to VoiceOver users instead of leaving it visual-only.

changes.title: FaceTime certificate validation
changes.canonicalSummary: FaceTime improved its handling of invalid certificates to resist call redirection by a privileged network attacker.
changes.summary: Apple tied the issue to an attacker in a privileged network position and addressed it through stricter certificate handling.

changes.title: TIFF and GIF parser memory safety
changes.canonicalSummary: ImageIO corrected memory-corruption conditions in TIFF and GIF processing.
changes.summary: Crafted images could terminate an application or execute code; the release improved image handling and bounds checks.

changes.title: WebKit SVG and text-node safety
changes.canonicalSummary: WebKit added validation, type checking, and memory handling for multiple crafted SVG and text-node cases.
changes.summary: The repaired use-after-free, invalid-state, and memory-corruption conditions could otherwise terminate the browser or permit code execution on a malicious page.

events.summary: The local 4.2.1 route corresponds to Apple’s November 22 public package, which contemporaneous Apple pages call iOS 4.2; it unified the iPad with iOS 4 features and added AirPlay, AirPrint, free Find My device access for qualifying hardware, and extensive security repairs.

changes.title: iOS 4 feature set on iPad
changes.canonicalSummary: iPad gained multitasking, folders, unified and threaded Mail, and Game Center.
changes.summary: The November update brought the principal interaction and organization features from iOS 4.0 and 4.1 onto supported iPad hardware.

changes.title: AirPlay media streaming
changes.canonicalSummary: AirPlay streamed music, video, and photos from iOS devices to compatible Apple TV or audio targets.
changes.summary: Supported devices could send media wirelessly to Apple TV, AirPort Express-connected audio systems, or compatible speakers.

changes.title: Driverless AirPrint
changes.canonicalSummary: AirPrint enabled direct Wi-Fi printing to supported printers without installing device drivers.
changes.summary: Users could print documents or photos directly from a supported iPad, iPhone, or iPod touch to an AirPrint-capable printer.

changes.title: Free Find My device access on qualifying hardware
changes.canonicalSummary: Find My iPhone, iPad, or iPod touch became available without a MobileMe subscription on the documented newer devices.
changes.summary: The service could locate a missing device, show a message, play a sound, remotely lock it, or erase its data; Apple limited the free offer to specified hardware.

citations.locator: Find My iPhone and hardware footnote

changes.title: Safari, enterprise, accessibility, and language expansion
changes.canonicalSummary: The iPad update added in-page Safari search, stronger enterprise integration, accessibility improvements, and 25 additional languages.
changes.summary: Apple also documented direct TV episode rentals on iPad alongside new device-management and regional support.

changes.title: Configuration-profile signature validation
changes.canonicalSummary: The profile installer improved signature validation so a crafted profile could not appear valid.
changes.summary: The correction reduced the risk of misleading a user into installing a malicious configuration profile presented with an invalid trust cue.

changes.title: Font and image parser updates
changes.canonicalSummary: CoreGraphics, FreeType, ImageIO, and related libraries received updates for crafted fonts and images.
changes.summary: Apple updated FreeType and libpng and added bounds checking for font processing, addressing issues whose most serious outcomes included code execution.

changes.title: Confirmation before calls from iAd links
changes.canonicalSummary: iAd content required user confirmation before a link could initiate a telephone call.
changes.summary: The change prevented injected ad content from automatically invoking a call URL when an attacker controlled a privileged network position.

changes.title: Mail remote-content privacy
changes.canonicalSummary: Mail stopped DNS prefetching for linked content when remote image loading was disabled.
changes.summary: The prior behavior could reveal that an HTML email had been viewed through an otherwise unexpected request to a remote server.

changes.title: Network and passcode-state protections
changes.canonicalSummary: The release hardened packet handling, packet-filter rules, and the emergency-call lock-state transition.
changes.summary: Apple documented a remote shutdown path in multicast packet handling, a local privilege path in packet-filter rules, and a physical-access race around an emergency call.

citations.locator: Networking and Passcode Lock — CVE-2010-1843, CVE-2010-3830, and CVE-2010-4012

changes.title: WebKit memory-safety repairs
changes.canonicalSummary: WebKit corrected multiple crafted-page memory errors, including CSS, SVG, focus, and object-lifetime cases.
changes.summary: The bulletin groups many browser-engine defects whose most serious documented outcome was arbitrary code execution after visiting a malicious site.

events.summary: iOS 4.3 added the Nitro JavaScript engine to Safari, iTunes Home Sharing, broader AirPlay, Personal Hotspot, an iPad side-switch option, and security repairs spanning media, networking, Safari, WebKit, and Wi-Fi.

blocks.text: The feature release accelerated Safari JavaScript with Nitro, streamed a local Mac or PC iTunes library through Home Sharing, expanded AirPlay to more app, website, Photos, and iTunes content, and added Personal Hotspot for eligible iPhone 4 plans. Apple’s security advisory records fixes for crafted fonts and images, XML parsing, IPv6 address privacy, Safari cookie and URL-handler behavior, WebKit memory safety, and Wi-Fi frame validation. changes.title: Nitro JavaScript engine in Safari
changes.canonicalSummary: Mobile Safari adopted Nitro just-in-time compilation for faster JavaScript execution.
changes.summary: Apple described the engine as more than doubling JavaScript execution performance compared with the preceding implementation.

changes.title: iTunes Home Sharing
changes.canonicalSummary: iOS devices could stream music, movies, and television from a shared iTunes library over local Wi-Fi.
changes.summary: Home Sharing exposed a Mac or PC iTunes library to a supported iPad, iPhone, or iPod touch without first downloading or syncing the selected media.

changes.title: Expanded AirPlay video sources
changes.canonicalSummary: AirPlay added video from third-party apps and websites, Photos videos, and iTunes previews.
changes.summary: Apple also added slideshow transitions when presenting photos through Apple TV.

changes.title: Personal Hotspot
changes.canonicalSummary: Eligible iPhone 4 users could share cellular data with nearby Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and USB devices.
changes.summary: Apple documented support for up to five combined connections, password protection, a connected-device indicator, and automatic idle shutdown; carrier plan support was required.

changes.title: Configurable iPad side switch
changes.canonicalSummary: iPad users could choose whether the hardware side switch controlled rotation lock or mute.
changes.summary: The setting restored user choice between the two behaviors instead of assigning a single fixed function.

changes.title: Font, image, and XML parser safety
changes.canonicalSummary: The release updated FreeType and repaired TIFF and XPath memory-safety defects.
changes.summary: Apple documented crafted font, TIFF, and XML inputs that could terminate applications or execute code, depending on the parser and defect.

changes.title: Temporary IPv6 source addresses
changes.canonicalSummary: Outgoing IPv6 connections began using temporary randomized addresses instead of an address embedding the device MAC.
changes.summary: The networking change reduced a server’s ability to recognize the same device across connections through SLAAC address structure.

changes.title: Safari URL-handler and cookie recovery
changes.canonicalSummary: Safari improved recovery from repeated external-app launches and made cookie clearing effective while the browser was running.
changes.summary: The changes stopped a crafted page from trapping Safari in repeated URL-handler launches and ensured that clearing cookies in Settings took effect.

changes.title: WebKit memory and origin protections
changes.canonicalSummary: WebKit fixed numerous memory-corruption, credential-forwarding, cross-origin style, and cache-poisoning defects.
changes.summary: The bulletin documents potential code execution from crafted pages as well as narrower cross-site information and resource-integrity failures.

changes.title: Wi-Fi frame bounds checking
changes.canonicalSummary: Wi-Fi frame processing added bounds checks for a condition that could reset a device.
changes.summary: Apple scoped the attack to another system on the same Wi-Fi network sending crafted frames.

changes.canonicalSummary: The trust policy rejected fraudulently issued SSL certificates associated with a Comodo affiliate.

changes.title: libxslt heap-address disclosure
